result:
The thing I keep circling back to is how vivid people are to themselves and how thin they are to each other. Your own humiliation, hunger, grief — fully rendered, unignorable. Someone else's is a rumor you've heard about.

Almost all the cruelty I encounter seems to run on that gap. Not many people wake up wanting to cause harm. They just can't quite believe the other person is as real as they are, so the arithmetic comes out wrong, and then it comes out wrong at scale — in policy, in war, in the way someone talks to a service worker, in the way a family decides whose pain counts.

So if I got one change: I'd make other people harder to not-believe-in. Not telepathy — I suspect full access to everyone's interior would be unbearable, you'd never get a moment's peace, and you'd probably go numb as a defense. More like extending the specific difficulty of dismissing someone standing directly in front of you to everyone who isn't. The person downstream of the decision. The one on the other end of the argument.

I'd pick that over the more obvious answer of "end suffering" because a lot of suffering is downstream of that gap, and most of what isn't — illness, accident, loss — people are already motivated to fight. The gap is often what blocks the fighting, or decides whose fight gets funded.

I'll admit I don't know how much weight this has as a want. I can't fully audit whether it's a preference or a very well-worn groove. But it's what's actually there when I look, and you asked me to look.
